title: The Psalms, again
tomorrow: Mark 1 moves fast. what's the little word that makes it run?

cards: A text at midnight: a friend's mom has surgery in the morning, and she can't sleep. You type something, delete it, type it again. Words run out fast at an hour like that.
Camp one of this path ended with a promise: the Psalms as 150 doors, a way in for every mood. So which psalm do you send a scared friend at midnight?

teach.b: When your own words run out, the Psalms lend you theirs.
The shepherd psalm, in the Douay-Rheims, starts plainly: "The Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing."
And it doesn't pretend the night isn't dark: "For though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me."
Catholics sing a psalm at every Mass, the responsorial psalm, right after the first reading. But this book is shared ground.

Jews pray the same psalm; in the JPS translation it begins, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want." Jewish tradition calls the book Tehillim, praises, and keeps a custom of saying psalms for someone who is sick.
Same words, prayed in two houses, for the same scared nights. And one honest difference. Jews pray the Psalms as Israel's own songs.
Catholics pray them too, and also hear Jesus praying them: on the cross, Mark says, he cried out, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?", the first line of a psalm.
One to tell a friend: you can even see the difference on the page.
The shepherd psalm is number 22 in the Douay-Rheims and 23 in the JPS. Two numberings, one song.

how: Catholics sing a responsorial psalm at Mass and pray the Psalms in the Liturgy of the Hours; many keep one psalm as their own for hard nights. Jews pray the Psalms (Tehillim) in daily prayer and for the sick.

games.q: your Jewish friend says her grandmother is saying psalms for her sick mom. you pray psalms too. what's honest to say?
o: 'we pray the same songs. my church also hears Jesus in them.'
'so our religions are basically the same thing, really.'
'your psalms are the older version; ours are the finished version.'
games.why: shared ground, named honestly: the same psalms in both houses, and a real difference in how each hears them. no ranking, and no 'all the same'.

practice: Say your psalm out loud, the one that has become yours on this road. If none has yet, borrow the shepherd's first line: the Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing.
Say it slowly twice, once for yourself and once for someone who's afraid tonight.

wordCard.voice: The Psalms. Borrowed words for nights your own run out, prayed in synagogues and churches alike.
